reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Typical features include central weight gain, a rounded plethoric face, a dorsocervical fat pad, thin skin, and easy bruising
Wide purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, and unexplained osteoporosis are among the more discriminating clinical signs
Exogenous glucocorticoid use is by far the most common cause and should be excluded by careful drug history before pursuing endogenous disease
Diagnosis proceeds in two stages: first confirm cortisol excess, then determine whether it is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent
Screening rests on demonstrating loss of normal cortisol regulation using late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
A suppressed ACTH points to an adrenal source, whereas a normal or elevated ACTH indicates a pituitary tumour or an ectopic source
Pituitary-dependent disease (Cushing disease) accounts for most endogenous ACTH-dependent cases, while ectopic ACTH is often from neuroendocrine tumours
Associated metabolic consequences include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, dyslipidaemia, and increased thrombotic and infection risk
Definitive management is directed at the underlying cause, most often surgical removal of the responsible tumour
reference.pathophysiology: Cushing syndrome results from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoid. This may be exogenous, from prescribed or surreptitious steroid use, or endogenous. Endogenous disease is divided into ACTH-dependent forms, in which a pituitary corticotroph adenoma or an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour drives adrenal cortisol output, and ACTH-independent forms, in which an adrenal adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral hyperplasia autonomously produces cortisol. Sustained cortisol excess disrupts the normal negative-feedback of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, abolishes the circadian rhythm of cortisol, and produces widespread catabolic, metabolic, immunosuppressive, and mineralocorticoid effects on multiple tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-Cushing states from severe obesity, depression, or heavy alcohol use
Poorly controlled diabetes with weight gain
additionalInvestigations: Late-night salivary cortisol to detect loss of the normal evening nadir
24-hour urinary free cortisol, ideally on more than one collection
Plasma ACTH to separate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease
Pituitary MRI, adrenal CT, or cross-sectional imaging for ectopic sources as directed by biochemistry
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise ACTH-dependent disease when imaging is equivocal
redFlags: Rapid onset with marked hypokalaemia and pigmentation suggesting aggressive ectopic ACTH secretion
New severe hypertension, hyperglycaemia, or thromboembolism from florid hypercortisolism
Features of adrenal carcinoma such as very high androgen or cortisol levels with a large adrenal mass
Severe proximal weakness, fractures, or psychosis reflecting advanced disease
reference.prognosis: With successful treatment of the underlying cause many features regress over months, though hypertension, bone loss, and psychological effects may persist; untreated hypercortisolism carries substantial cardiovascular, metabolic, infective, and thrombotic mortality, and ectopic ACTH from malignancy has a poor outlook.
pitfalls: Overlooking exogenous steroid exposure, including inhaled, topical, or injected preparations
Interpreting a single borderline test as diagnostic rather than repeating and combining screening tests
Confusing pseudo-Cushing states with true disease during acute illness, depression, or alcohol excess
Assuming a pituitary microadenoma on imaging proves the source without confirmatory biochemistry
